item.question: A stand has 20 cycles, some bicycles and some tricycles, with 46 wheels in all. How many of each?
steps: Let t be the number of tricycles, so there are 20 − t bicycles.
Wheels: 3t + 2(20 − t) = 46, so t + 40 = 46 and t is 6.
There are 6 tricycles and 14 bicycles. Check: 3 × 6 + 2 × 14 = 18 + 28 = 46.
Without letters: 20 bicycles would have 40 wheels; each tricycle adds 1 more, and 46 − 40 = 6.

concept_name: Undo a chain of doubling and giving away

item.question: Asha has some stickers. She doubles them and gives away 5, then doubles again and gives away 5. She has 13 left. How many did she start with?
steps: Let x be the start. After round one she has 2x − 5.
After round two she has 2(2x − 5) − 5, which is 4x − 15.
So 4x − 15 = 13, which gives 4x = 28 and x is 7.

item.text:

1. Let the price be p rupees. Income is 60p.
2. Costs: rent 200 and making 60 × 5 = 300.
3. Profit: 60p − 300 − 200 = 400, so 60p = 900 and p is 15.
4. Check: 60 × 15 = 900, and 900 − 300 − 200 = 400.
Answer: ₹15 per glass

steps_tex: $(1 + 3) \div (5 + 7) = 4 \div 12$, which is one third.
$(1 + 3 + 5) \div (7 + 9 + 11) = 9 \div 27$, which is one third again.
The first $n$ odd numbers add up to $n \times n$, and the first $2n$ odd numbers add up to $4 \times n \times n$.
So the next $n$ odd numbers add up to $4 \times n \times n$ minus $n \times n$, which is $3 \times n \times n$, three times the top.
item.answer_tex: Every fraction equals one third, because the bottom sum is always three times the top sum

After the third round the coins doubled, and he was left with only 8 coins, exactly the number he owed the genie. (i) How many coins did Karim initially have? (ii) For what cost per round should Karim agree to the deal, if he wants to increase the number of coins he has? (iii) Through its magical powers, the genie knows the number of coins that Karim has. How should the genie set the cost per round so that it gets all of Karim's coins?
steps_tex: (i): Let $x$ be the start. After one round $2x - 8$, after two rounds $4x - 24$.
The third doubling gives $8x - 48$, which is $8$, so $8x = 56$ and $x$ is $7$.
Check: $7$, then $14 - 8 = 6$, then $12 - 8 = 4$, then $8$, all given to the genie.

(ii): With cost $c$, one round turns $x$ into $2x - c$, which is more than $x$ only when $c$ is less than $x$. So Karim should agree only if the cost is less than the coins he starts with, here fewer than $7$.
(iii): After three rounds he has $8x - 7c$. For this to be $0$, the genie sets $c$ to $8x \div 7$. For $7$ coins that is $8$ per round, exactly the genie's trick.
